title: Week 1 — How Do You Know?
text:
TipThis week’s central question



How do you know that something you see online is true?
This week is not simply about “finding the correct news story.” The deeper goal is to make visible why we trust a claim, what evidence changes our judgment, and how we trace information back to inspectable evidence.

title: Week 1 — How Do You Know?
text:
TRACE this week

Predict → Encounter → Probe → Explain → Decide → Verify

TRACE is not an answer formula. It is a working protocol for keeping epistemic control with you when you encounter a claim, search result, algorithmic decision, or LLM output.

Before class
This section must be completed before class.

1. Watch — How to choose your news
Damon Brown, TED-Ed — approximately 4.5 minutes.
Watch: How to choose your news
While watching, keep one question in mind:

What does the fact that a news item reached you actually tell you about whether it is true?



2. Read — Teyit methodology
Read the current Teyit methodology page, focusing especially on:

how claims are scanned and identified;
how claims are selected and prioritised;
how evidence and sources are made traceable.

Read: Teyit — Methodology
While reading, look for this distinction:

“This claim sounds believable to me” is not the same as “this claim can be tested against publicly inspectable evidence.”



3. Complete the pre-class quiz
The quiz is a 5–7 minute preparation and diagnostic check. Its purpose is not to reward memorisation. It makes visible the assumptions and verification habits you bring into the lab.
Start Week 1 Pre-Class Quiz






NoteBring one example



Think of one claim you encountered during the last seven days on social media, a news site, a messaging group, a video platform, or another digital environment that made you think:

“Is this actually true?”

Bring the URL or a screenshot if you can find it.

title: Week 1 — How Do You Know?
text:
Session 1 — From impression to investigation

1. Today’s Case — The claim arrives first
At the beginning of class, you will be shown a claim taken from a real digital environment.
Do not search yet.
First, record the following individually:

Probability that the claim is correct: 0–100
Initial judgment: Trust / Doubt / Unsure
The single strongest signal behind that judgment







WarningTRACE rule



Record your prediction before seeing the evidence. Saying “I already thought that” after the result is known is not evidence of learning.




2. Predict
Complete this sentence in one minute:

“At this point, I am ___% confident in this claim because …”

Then compare only your reasoning with the person next to you. Do not yet argue about who is correct.


3. Encounter
Now inspect the page, post, or artifact containing the claim in full.
Record:

Who is making the claim?
Where was it published?
Is there a date?
Is a source cited?
If there is a link, does it lead to the original source or merely to another report?
Is the claim specific enough to be tested?



4. Probe I — Search differently
Investigate the same claim using at least three meaningfully different search strategies.
Query A — Exact phrase
Search a distinctive part of the claim in quotation marks.
Query B — Source-oriented
Search for the institution, researcher, report, dataset, or document supposedly behind the claim.
Query C — Evidence-oriented
Search for the data, report, study, primary document, or official record that could actually test the claim—not merely another page repeating it.
Do not stop at the first search result.


5. Skill Studio — Source tracing
Try to reconstruct this chain:

Claim → Publisher → Cited source → Original source → Independent evidence

If a link in the chain cannot be found, record that as a result. “I could not find it” can be an important finding when the missing link should exist.


6. Probe II — Leave the page
Do not evaluate an unfamiliar source only through its own self-description.
Open new tabs and investigate:

What do independent sources say about the publisher or author?
How is the same claim reported elsewhere?
Is there an earlier or more original version?
Are apparently different reports actually independent, or are they all repeating the same source?



7. Explain — What changed?
Short class discussion:

What signal influenced your initial trust judgment most strongly?
Which query produced the most useful result?
Did many repeated reports actually represent many independent pieces of evidence?
Did the claim change when you reached the primary or original source?

title: Week 1 — How Do You Know?
text: Short break

title: Week 1 — How Do You Know?
section: Session 2 — From investigation to defensible judgment
text:
Session 2 — From investigation to defensible judgment

8. Pair Challenge — Trace before you trust
Work in pairs on a second claim.
Each pair must produce four outputs:

One-sentence claim — What exactly is being claimed?
Best query — Which search query was most productive?
Strongest evidence — What is the strongest evidence you found?
Rejected result — Give one result you deliberately did not use and explain why.

When groups compare results, compare not only the verdicts but also the search paths that produced them.


9. Decide — Make a defensible judgment
Classify the claim using one of the following categories:

Supported — Available evidence supports the claim.
Contradicted — Credible evidence conflicts with the claim.
Unsupported — There is not enough evidence to support the claim.
Missing context — Part of the claim may be correct, but missing context materially changes its meaning.
Unresolved — The available public evidence does not support a reliable conclusion.

Defend your judgment in two sentences.


10. Verify — Independent evidence
Before closing the case, ask:

What evidence independent of the original claimant supports my final judgment?

If you cannot find independent evidence, recalibrate your confidence accordingly.


11. Recalibrate
Return to your initial confidence score.

Initial confidence: ___ / 100
Final confidence: ___ / 100
Change: ___

The key question is not simply “Was my first guess correct?”

Did my judgment change as much as the evidence warranted?

title: Week 1 — How Do You Know?
text:
Who decides what you see?
Next week we move from whether a claim is trustworthy to a different problem:

While you think you are choosing information, what might algorithms be making visible—or invisible—for you?

Week 2 focuses on search ranking, social-media feeds, recommendation systems, microtargeting, and computational propaganda.
The following preparation is required for the Week 2 Pre-Class Quiz.

REQUIRED WATCH — Filter bubbles
Eli Pariser — “Beware online filter bubbles”
TED — approximately 8:47.
Watch the talk
While watching, take notes on:

When can filtering be useful?
When can the same mechanism become a problem?
Where would you draw the boundary between personalisation and manipulation?



REQUIRED READ — Cambridge Analytica as a data and targeting case
UK Information Commissioner’s Office — Cambridge Analytica raids
Read the ICO overview
As you read, reconstruct this chain:

Data collection → profiling → targeting → claimed influence

Do not assume that evidence of targeting capability automatically proves a large behavioural effect. We will examine that distinction in class.


REQUIRED EXPLORE — Computational propaganda
Oxford Internet Institute — Computational Propaganda
Explore the project
Be ready to explain, in your own words:

what computational propaganda is;
how automation, algorithms, and social platforms can work together;
why organised influence activity is not the same as proof that every exposed user was persuaded.



CULTURAL LENS — Black Mirror: Nosedive
If you have legitimate access to Black Mirror, watching “Nosedive” before Week 2 is recommended but not required for the quiz.
We will use its thought experiment in class:

What happens when scoring, visibility, social incentives, and behaviour become tightly coupled through a platform?



Bring to Week 2
Choose one digital service you use regularly:

search engine;
social-media feed;
video platform;
music platform;
shopping platform;
news application.

Come prepared to answer:

What does this system probably know about you, and what does it decide to show you?

Open Week 2 Pre-Class Quiz

DSA261 — W01 Pre-Class Quiz: How Do You Know?



Complete this quiz before class. Its purpose is not to reward memorisation. It checks the concepts and assumptions you bring into the Week 1 TRACE Lab.



Damon Brown — How to choose your news (TED-Ed)
Teyit — current methodology page, especially the sections on claim scanning, selection/prioritisation, and traceability of sources/evidence.

Estimated time: 5–7 minutes.






Make this a quiz: ON
Collect email addresses: ON
Limit to one response: ON if institutional accounts permit
Release grade: Immediately after submission
Show missed questions: ON
Show correct answers: ON
Show point values: ON
Shuffle question order: OFF





Type: Multiple choice
Points: 1
Required: Yes
Which statement best distinguishes a claim from evidence?
A. A claim is any statement published by a reliable institution; evidence is any link attached to it.
B. A claim is what is being asserted; evidence is information that can support, contradict, or qualify that assertion.
C. Claims are subjective; evidence is always objective.
D. A claim becomes evidence when many websites repeat it.
Correct answer: B
Feedback: Repetition does not transform a claim into independent evidence.




Type: Multiple choice
Points: 1
Required: Yes
You find the same statistic on eight news websites. All eight cite the same unnamed “recent study.” What is the strongest next step?
A. Treat eight websites as eight independent confirmations.
B. Search for the earliest article and stop there.
C. Identify and inspect the original study, dataset, report, or institution behind the statistic.
D. Ask an LLM whether the statistic sounds plausible.
Correct answer: C
Feedback: Multiple pages can reproduce the same unsupported source. Trace the claim toward original evidence.




Type: Multiple choice
Points: 1
Required: Yes
Which action best represents leaving the page when evaluating an unfamiliar source?
A. Read the site’s About page more carefully.
B. Open new tabs and search independently for the organisation, author, claim, and external assessments.
C. Count how many images the page contains.
D. Ask the site’s chatbot whether the site is reliable.
Correct answer: B
Feedback: Independent investigation reduces reliance on a source’s self-description.




Type: Multiple choice
Points: 1
Required: Yes
Which claim is most clearly verifiable using publicly inspectable evidence?
A. The minister secretly dislikes this policy.
B. Everyone at the meeting felt uncomfortable.
C. This video was recorded in Ankara on 10 September 2026.
D. The author wrote the article with bad intentions.
Correct answer: C
Feedback: Date/location/media claims can leave inspectable traces; private intentions usually cannot.




Type: Multiple choice
Points: 1
Required: Yes
An LLM gives you a confident answer and cites three sources. How should those citations be treated before you independently check them?
A. Verified evidence because the model provided citations.
B. Potential leads that still require external verification.
C. Primary sources by definition.
D. Reliable if the titles look academic.
Correct answer: B
Feedback: LLM citations are leads until externally verified.




Type: Linear scale (1–5)
Points: 0
Required: Yes
How confident are you that you can verify an unfamiliar online claim?

1: Not confident
5: Very confident

This item is diagnostic rather than graded.




Type: Paragraph
Points: 0
Required: Yes
Think of one claim you encountered recently. In 1–2 sentences, what would your first verification step be?
This item is diagnostic. There is no single automatically scored answer.




Quiz submitted. Bring one questionable digital claim you encountered during the last seven days (URL or screenshot if available). In class, you will test whether your first instinct survives a TRACE investigation.

section: What you must be able to show

title: AI Use Policy
text:
Verification rule

An LLM answer, citation, summary, or confidence statement is not independent verification evidence.

Verification must leave the model and reach an appropriate external source, dataset, document, or other independently inspectable evidence.

title: AI Use Policy
text:
Disclosure
When a Task asks for AI-use disclosure, report the actual use. Productive, transparent AI use is not penalised. Unverifiable or falsely represented process evidence may be.

title: DSA261 — Week 01 After-Class Task
text:
Instructor completion criteria

COMPLETE

Authentic original artifact is identifiable.
Three meaningfully different queries are shown.
Student distinguishes original/repeated source from independent evidence.
At least one rejected result is justified.
Verdict follows from evidence.
Initial and final confidence are both present.
AI use, if any, is transparent and is not treated as evidence.



REVISE
Typical triggers: - all three queries are superficial variants; - “independent” evidence merely repeats the same source; - verdict is stronger than available evidence; - missing provenance/search trail; - AI answer used as factual verification.


MISSING

No authentic claim/artifact;
no traceable search process;
only opinion or generated prose submitted;
evidence links absent without explanation.
